newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Orthodox Church lukewarm on Pope visit to Romania.
newsitem.headline: Orthodox Church lukewarm on Pope visit to Romania.

text.p: Romania's mainstream Orthodox Church said on Wednesday a proposed visit by Pope John Paul would first require progress in settling a longstanding dispute with minority Greek Catholics.

"We don't oppose a visit by His Holiness the Pope. But for this visit to take place, we need peace and reconciliation with the Greek Catholic Church.," Liviu Stoina, adviser to the Orthodox Patriarch's office, told Reuters.
"We have repeatedly called for reconciliation with the Greek Catholic Church. But the reaction of our Greek Catholic brothers has been discouraging for us."

Foreign Minister Adrian Severin, who arrived in Italy for a four-day visit on Tuesday, told Reuters before leaving he would deliver an invitation to John Paul to make the first visit by a Pope to Romania.
He said leaders of the Orthodox Church, which claims the allegiance of 86 percent of Romania's 22 million people, had dropped their objections to a papal visit.
"Representatives of the Romanian Orthodox Church have recently expressed a wish for the pope's visit to take place," Severin said.

"They asked for the visit to be used in order to prepare the reconciliation between the two churches. This is the only Latin Orthodox church in the world and it is definitely not a fundamentalist church."
Only about 1.2 million Romanians, or some five percent of the population, are Roman Catholics in eastern Europe's only country speaking a Latin language.
A further 223,000, mainly in the central Transylvania region, are Greek Catholics, who accept the Pope's authority but practise Eastern Orthodox rites.

Romania's communist authorities banned the Greek Catholic church after World War Two, as did Josef Stalin in neighbouring Soviet Ukraine, where the church claims five million followers in the post-Communist era. Property in both countries was confiscated and turned over to the Orthodox Church.
The Greek Catholic church was re-legalised in Romania after the 1989 fall of communism, but governments have yet to tackle the thorny issue of returning 2,500 churches and other assets.
The new centrist government, which ousted ex-communists in general elections last November, sees an invitation to the Pope as a boost to its campaign to win friends in the West.

Greek Catholics holding Sunday mass outside their former churches are a common sight across Transylvania and disputes have occasionally spilled over into battles pitting worshippers against one another.
There has been little progress on draft legislation to return church assets confiscated by communists. The bill would also rule on lost mosques and synagogues.
